papers.title: What Language Adds, and at What Cost: Four Controlled Probes of Pathology Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision--language models (VLMs) promise to make computational pathology queryable and able to draft reports, but how much language adds beyond the vision backbone is unclear, because almost every system is evaluated by its developers on test sets of their own choosing. We grade published evidence by how it was produced and test four claims with controlled probes that reuse released checkpoints and public data, varying one input at a time. Report text adds prognostic signal: adding a frozen embedding of the stage-redacted report to a slide embedding raises the pooled C-index by 0.019 for progression-free interval and by 0.016 for overall survival across 1{,}633 TCGA patients, and restoring the stage statement adds nothing. Prompts add no measurable accuracy at inference: with features and pooling fixed, zero-shot classification is statistically indistinguishable from a supervised linear probe for lung and renal cancer subtyping. Slide-level question answering is barely grounded: SlideChat answers 74.82\% of SlideBench-VQA(TCGA) items correctly with the slide and 74.41\% without it, whereas its language backbone alone reaches 43.52\%. Paraphrasing leaves accuracy unchanged but flips 8--23\% of answers. Self-reported gains from agentic navigation and few-shot language priors cannot yet be attributed to language. Language thus adds real but narrow value, and we propose minimum controls that would expose these failure modes in future evaluations.

papers.title: High-dimensional covariate-assisted ranking
papers.abstract: Ranking data in modern applications often involves covariate vectors whose dimension grows with the number of objects. Identifying relevant covariates and integrating them with item-specific utilities can yield better predictive performance. In this work, we study a Plackett--Luce model that incorporates both item-specific utilities and high-dimensional covariate effects. Under a sparsity assumption on the covariate coefficients, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for identifiability in terms of the Kruskal rank of the restricted covariate design. We then propose an $\ell_1$-regularized maximum likelihood estimator for the covariate coefficients. Under suitable design and connectivity conditions, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the estimator with probability tending to one, as well as its uniform consistency. With an additional minimum-signal condition, we further establish exact support recovery. Our analysis combines a hypergraph-based chaining technique with a profile-likelihood perturbation analysis, yielding estimation rates that explicitly capture the effects of the comparison hypergraph's connectivity and the underlying sparsity level. Numerical experiments using synthetic data and a horse racing dataset corroborate our theoretical findings.

papers.title: Physics-Constrained Modeling and Inference of the Equation of State for Dissociative Materials
papers.abstract: Equations of state (EOSs) describe how a material's internal energy and pressure change with temperature and density. They are inputs to hydrodynamic simulations in materials science and planetary science. We model the ion-thermal free-energy term for dissociative materials, where molecular bonds break apart to form new species under extreme conditions. This term is governed by two latent physical processes, a molar-mass surface and a Debye-temperature curve, neither of which is observed directly. Instead, both must be recovered from internal energy and pressure, which are derivatives of the free energy, subject to thermodynamic constraints. Existing EOS tables are typically built through material-specific hand-tuning, a process that is tedious, does not scale across materials or conditions, and offers no guarantee of thermodynamic consistency. We propose a partitioned statistical framework that infers molar mass and Debye temperature directly from EOS data, guaranteeing thermodynamic consistency by construction. Local molar-mass behavior is captured with polynomial basis functions across domain partitions, while the Debye temperature is modeled with an I-spline basis. In simulations and a carbon dioxide case study, the method accurately recovers the underlying physical quantities, improves prediction of held-out energy and pressure data, and provides uncertainty quantification while scaling with EOS table size.

papers.title: Dirichlet-Tree Allocation Priors for Bayesian Causal Forests
papers.abstract: Bayesian Causal Forests (BCF) estimate heterogeneous treatment effects with a separate ensemble of treatment trees. The prior on the leaf values of the treatment trees determines whether sampling variability is attributed to the treatment effect. Independent shrinkage priors exert no control over how a tree allocates variability across its leaves, and their total prior variance grows as leaves are added. We propose the Dirichlet-Tree Bayesian Causal Forest, which jointly regularizes the leaf values of each treatment tree through a Dirichlet-Tree prior on their variance shares, generated by stick-breaking along the tree topology. We characterize the spike and tails of the marginal leaf prior, show that the prior adaptively bounds the number of regions of effect heterogeneity, and establish posterior consistency for the forest. In simulations, the model outperforms BCF when heterogeneity is confined to a few regions and reduces spurious heterogeneity elsewhere, and, unlike independent shrinkage priors, its accuracy does not deteriorate as the trees grow. We also evaluate the model on real data, including a pancreatic cancer survival study.

papers.title: Bombadil: A Foundation Model for Plant Electrophysiology
papers.abstract: Living plants, like animals, use electrical signals to carry information about their physiological state across their body, from roots to branches. These signals can be recorded, as they are in animals, from a pair of differential extracellular electrodes inserted into signal-conducting tissue. While machine-learning models have been trained to predict specific plant stress states from these signals, each of these models has been trained for only a single task and none have been designed to transfer across tasks, species, or environments. These approaches do not allow easy scaling across the wide range of species and environments that are relevant to agriculture, forestry, and horticulture for both commercial and consumer plant care. Here we present Bombadil, a foundation model for plant electrophysiology, pretrained without labels on over 4 million hours of electrical signals recorded from 100 plant species in ten distinct environments, including laboratories, greenhouses, commercial orchards, and natural forests. In this way, Bombadil is able to learn the fundamental features of plant electrical signals across a wide array of species and environments. Then, from those same electrical signals, Bombadil tracks changes in seven physiological indicators of plant stress, even among species and stressors with no labels in training.

papers.title: Synthetic Control: An Exact Geometric Formulation
papers.abstract: The synthetic control method matches a treated unit to a convex combination of donor units, with the relative importance of each predictor determined by a weight matrix $V$. In standard practice, $V$ is selected through a bi-level optimization problem that is nonconvex and lacks convergence guarantees. This article derives an exact geometric solution for synthetic control estimators. For any positive definite $V$, a synthetic control is given by the projection of the treated unit's predictors onto the convex hull of the donor predictors under a $V$-weighted norm. As $V$ varies over its candidate class, these projections trace out the set of attainable synthetic controls. We characterize this set. When the predictor vector of the treated unit lies outside the convex hull of the donor predictors, the attainable set under general positive definite $V$ is the union of the facets of the donor hull that are visible from the treated unit. For diagonal $V$, a sign-compatibility test identifies the attainable set. When the treated unit lies inside the hull, exact matches exist. We select the one that minimizes the average of the pairwise matching discrepancies between the treated unit and each of the donors contributing to the synthetic control. These characterizations replace bi-level optimization with a fast enumeration method that is guaranteed to deliver the global optimum over the attainable set. Moreover, the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions for the selection of donor weights characterize the set of positive definite predictor weight matrices that rationalize any given set of donor weights. Applications to the California tobacco control program and to the economic effects of German reunification illustrate the advantages of the proposed procedure over existing practice.

papers.title: Small Average Error, Wide Individual Error: General-Purpose LLMs Estimating Energy Intake from Meal Photos in a Feeding Trial
papers.abstract: Photo-based estimation of food energy could ease dietary assessment, and general-purpose multimodal large language models (LLMs) make such estimates easy to obtain. Most evaluations use one photo taken before eating and compare with energy served, while dietary assessment needs energy eaten. We evaluated six models from two vendors (Claude Haiku, Sonnet and Opus 5.5; GPT-6 luna, 6.1 sol and 6 astra) on 802 meals from ACETADA, a controlled feeding trial with weighed intake, with the before photo only, before and after photos in separate calls (subtraction), or both photos in one request. Three results ran against intuition. Subtraction under-estimated intake for five of six models, because the models still report hundreds of kilocalories for a nearly empty tray. Scaling the before-only estimate by the average share eaten (0.87) matched much of the gain from the after photo; beyond that constant, the second photo lowered meal-level error by only 2.2 to 3.4 points, mainly in meals with food left. With one photo, two models had a near-zero intake bias only because they under-estimated the served energy and ignored uneaten food. In ablations, adding the after photo improved accuracy under both prompt formats for five models, while prompt effects varied across models. Over 148 feeding days, three models kept the 90% confidence interval of their mean error within a pre-set 10% margin, but no model reached the pre-set 30% limits of agreement. Protein was under-estimated by every model, most in protein-dense meals; repeated calls changed error by at most 1.4 points; a high reasoning effort helped only the smallest model (4.2 points) and changed the others by less than 1 point. A low average bias is not evidence of accurate individual intake estimation; such estimates should support, not replace, assessment by a dietitian.

papers.title: R2-GP: Variance-Calibrated Priors for Additive Gaussian Processes
papers.abstract: We develop R2-GP, an R2D2-type prior for Gaussian process (GP) generalised additive models (GAMs) that calibrates explained variance ($R^2$) for Matérn covariance kernels. The function variance for standard Matérn kernels depends jointly on the effect magnitude and length-scale. As such, smooth and rough components with identical amplitudes contribute very different amounts of variation. With independent priors on component amplitudes, this variation results in variance overestimation, especially in higher dimensions. We overcome this by taking direct control over each component's expected contribution to prior explained variance. We do this by rescaling each component based on its length scale and observed inputs, and modelling each rescaled variance as a share of the function variance induced by a global $R^2$ prior. This allows R2-GP to scale well to many components. To also scale to large sample sizes, we extend R2-GP to Hilbert space approximation methods, a framework for kernels exploiting their spectral decompositions for fast and efficient inference. Our simulations and real-world case studies demonstrate superior generalisation and parameter recovery over independent variance priors.

papers.title: Almost Uniform Bias Correction for Persistent Panel Local Projections
papers.abstract: Panel local projections are widely used to estimate impulse responses in policy analysis. This paper examines the properties of the fixed-effect estimator and various bias-correction methods in panel local projections, focusing on settings with autoregressive control variables. We analyze the bias and variance of these estimators while allowing for persistence in both the target and control variables. Our theoretical findings indicate that the half-panel jackknife has desirable bias-reducing properties beyond the stationary setup. For empirical researchers, we recommend using bias-correction-adjusted standard errors to account for the sampling uncertainty associated with the half-panel jackknife estimator, regardless of the time-series dimension of the data.

papers.title: Simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation for stochastic reaction networks
papers.abstract: Uncovering stochastic reaction networks from data is central to single-cell biology. Simulation-based inference has evolved into a flexible paradigm for this purpose, circumventing the computational intractability of the likelihood. Notably, approximate Bayesian computation performs this inference by carrying out extensive Gillespie simulations, usually at a high computational cost. Here, we propose a simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation (SFABC) framework that avoids both simulation and explicit likelihood solutions of the network dynamics. Instead, SFABC exploits the Chemical Master Equation to formulate a tractable convex optimization with ensuing constraints, which are then used to accept sampled parameters consistent with the observed data. The resulting posterior approximation comes with theoretical guarantees: it can be tightened systematically, and it provably converges to the exact Bayesian posterior distributions. Using synthetic benchmarks, we show that SFABC matches the accuracy of standard simulation-based algorithms at a substantially reduced computational cost. We then showcase the applicability of SFABC to experimental systems biology by analyzing gene transcription bursting kinetics from snapshot, time-resolved, and cell-cycle-resolved single-cell data.

papers.title: Quantifying Uncertainty Bounds in Spectral Shallow Water Bathymetry: The Profile Likelihood Framework for Semi-Analytical Models
papers.abstract:
Accurate bathymetric mapping in shallow waters is critical for coastal monitoring, navigation safety, and environmental conservation. While semi-analytical (SA) models have proven effective for estimating water column depth (WCD) from optical remote sensing data, quantifying the associated uncertainties remains a significant challenge. This study introduces a unified framework based on profile likelihood to evaluate WCD uncertainties in Semi-Analytical (SA) models, bridging traditional variance-covariance methods with likelihood-based inference. Through controlled simulations, we systematically assess the performance of first-order statistical tests-likelihood ratio, Wald (observed and expected), and score tests-across varying environmental conditions and sensor configurations.

Our results demonstrate that the expected Fisher information Wald test, equivalent to classical variance-covariance propagation, provides reliable uncertainty bounds in hyperspectral settings with clear waters. However, its performance deteriorates in multispectral applications and complex water conditions, where likelihood ratio tests prove more robust. This divergence highlights fundamental limitations in the small-sample regime typical of per-pixel spectral bathymetry. Notably, even under idealized conditions with true parameter initialization, local optimization challenges in SA models can compromise both parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification, suggesting even greater challenges in practical applications with less favorable initialization. The findings underscore the importance of robust statistical inference in improving the reliability of bathymetric products for operational applications.

papers.title: Incorporating therapist capacity, availability and turnover in trials of therapist-delivered interventions: Non-orthogonal factorial designs
papers.abstract: Disentangling therapist from intervention effects has long been considered a challenge in randomised trials of therapist delivered interventions. When separating these effects is of interest, factorial designs have been proposed in which therapists and interventions are regarded as two potentially interacting components of a complex intervention, represented by two treatment factors (one random, one fixed). In these trial designs, every therapist delivers each intervention, and patients are randomised to the resulting therapist intervention combinations. It is assumed that each therapist is allocated the same number of patients (equal capacity), that all therapists in a centre are available when a patient is randomised (equal availability), and that therapists remain involved for the entire duration of the trial (no turnover). In practice, these are strong assumptions that may lead to delayed or suspended randomisation and increased trial costs. We propose three novel randomisation strategies that explicitly account for therapist capacity, availability, and turnover while maintaining desirable statistical properties. In a simulation study, we compared the proposed and existing randomisation strategies across trial scenarios and design parameters, assessing trade offs between operational efficiency and statistical performance. The results provide practical guidance for trialists designing trials of therapist delivered interventions under real world constraints.

papers.title: PyGPLA: A Python Package for Generalized Phase Locking Analysis
papers.abstract: Spike-field couplings measure the links between neuronal spiking and local field potential (LFP) and provide a tool to study how neural populations coordinate activity across spatial and temporal scales. While modern high-density electrophysiology enables the simultaneous recording of numerous LFP channels and neuronal units, this massive scale poses significant statistical and computational challenges for conventional pairwise coupling analyses. The number of channel-unit comparisons grows rapidly, and a coherent population-level structure can be obscured by high-dimensional coupling matrices. Generalized Phase Locking Analysis (GPLA) addresses this challenge by organizing spike-triggered LFP phase information into a complex coupling matrix and extracting dominant low-rank modes. These modes summarize whether a population is coupled to the field, which channels and units contribute to the coupling, and how their relative phases are organized. Here, we present PyGPLA, an open-source Python package implementing GPLA for high-density electrophysiological recordings. Designed for straightforward integration into existing neural data analysis pipelines, PyGPLA supports multivariate spike-LFP coupling analysis, from coupling estimation and interpretation to significance assessment using analytical and surrogate-based tests.

papers.title: Deep-$π^*$: A Neural Network Estimate of Trend Inflation
papers.abstract: Most empirical models of trend inflation treat it as a latent random walk driven by unobserved shocks, so they cannot say which economic conditions move it. Deep-$π^*$ makes the innovations to the trend a possibly nonlinear function of a large number of macroeconomic indicators, estimated with neural networks, so that Shapley values can be used to attribute every movement of the trend to the indicators behind it. Two complementary loss functions define a current trend, which fits inflation today, and a forward-looking trend, which best predicts inflation over the next year. In US data, employment-related variables were the largest contributors to the post-pandemic rise of the current trend. However, the forward-looking trend rose earlier, with real activity, employment, and money and credit as the main drivers, and peaked eight to twelve months before the current trend. Both trends looked through most of the movements in energy and commodity prices. The contributions of the indicators are nonlinear, with sizeable interactions between them. Re-estimated every month during the surge, the model forecast inflation more accurately than the standard UC-SV model and a random walk, and in early 2021, when professional forecasters expected inflation of 3% or less, the forward-looking trend was already signalling an increase in persistent inflation.

papers.title: A Pitfall in the Evaluation of Gene Perturbation Models
papers.abstract: Gene perturbation models aim to predict transcriptional responses to unseen genetic interventions, but comparisons rely on heterogeneous evaluation metrics and differentially-expressed (DE) gene subsets. We investigate the consequences of these choices using eight methods across six single-gene perturbation datasets under a unified evaluation protocol. Varying the number of top DE genes reveals substantial instability in Precision-based rankings, with the winning method changing $86.7\%$ of the time, while rankings based on the rest of the metrics remain comparatively stable. Investigating this discrepancy exposes that repeating a single predicted expression profile across cell-level rows, a standard practice for many methods, can inflate significance estimates and produce excessively large predicted significant-DE sets. Specifically we found that $67.1\%$ of tested perturbation--gene pairs pass the significance threshold despite some of them having minuscule effects. We derive an inflation factor showing that replicated predictions can amplify the standardized Mann--Whitney statistic even after correction for tied ranks, without adding independent information. This artifact changes Precision mainly as the number of DE genes increases because for smaller cutoffs, most of the genes are already significant due to the effect-based ordering. Taking this pitfall into account in our benchmark comparison, we find that a random forest using Gene Ontology features achieves the best overall results.

papers.title: Covariate-adaptive randomization using historical data and bootstrap-based inference
papers.abstract: Covariate-adaptive randomization (CAR) can improve the efficiency of average treatment effect (ATE) estimation by reducing chance imbalances in prognostic baseline covariates. A recently proposed CAR method that balances multiple covariates, including continuous ones, can achieve optimal precision when the conditional mean of the outcome can be expressed as a linear combination of the covariate features used for the CAR procedure. However, this condition may be difficult to satisfy when the relationship between covariates and the outcome is nonlinear. Furthermore, directly balancing multiple covariates may reduce estimation precision in finite samples. We propose three CAR methods that incorporate a prognostic score learned from individual-level historical data into their imbalance measures. The prognostic score reduces multiple covariates to one dimension while giving larger weights to covariates that are more strongly associated with the outcome. Another challenge with CAR is difficulty in inference due to dependence between subjects induced by the CAR procedure. Existing bootstrap-based inference methods emulate the CAR design by reassigning treatment within each bootstrap sample, which causes difficulty in interval estimation under CAR with continuous covariates. We propose a bootstrap method with unequal probability resampling corresponding to the CAR design, avoiding reassignment within each bootstrap sample. In simulations, the proposed CAR methods reduced prognostic imbalance, thereby improving estimation precision compared to existing assignment designs, and the proposed bootstrap method accurately assessed estimation uncertainty under our proposed CAR. An application to Clazosentan trials demonstrated that the proposed CAR methods similarly improved prognostic balance, and the proposed bootstrap method closely reproduced the distribution induced by the proposed CAR.

papers.title: Causal Robustness from Synthetic Environments
papers.abstract: We study robust prediction when the training data come from a single observational distribution. Causality-oriented methods for robust prediction usually use heterogeneity across observed environments both to learn an invariant prediction function and to determine the perturbations against which it is robust. We show that both can be recovered from one distribution under a structural additive-noise mechanism for the response. Under the structural model considered here, the causal prediction function has constant conditional mean squared error given its prediction. We generate synthetic environments by reweighting the covariate distribution along the prediction and use a Cramér--von Mises criterion to measure departures from this invariance. The resulting penalised risk admits a regularised worst-case representation, linking the criterion to robustness against covariate shifts induced by reweighting observations according to their predicted values. Under an additional orthogonality condition, we identify the causal prediction function as the unique risk minimiser subject to this invariance restriction. We establish consistency and an explicit rate, derive a goodness-of-fit test for the invariance restriction, and characterise the population target under misspecification. With multiple observed environments, the construction applies environment by environment and can be combined with Distributional Robustness via Invariant Gradients (DRIG) to control two complementary classes of shifts.

papers.title: Depth based on translates of a convex body: geometry, floating bodies, and empirical theory
papers.abstract: For a fixed full-dimensional convex body $K\subset\mathbb R^d$, we study the $K$-depth of a point $y$ with respect to a probability measure $μ$ by comparing the masses of translates of $K$ that fail to contain $y$. Its upper level sets are intersections of high-mass translates of $K$, and hence are convex and admit an exact representation as Minkowski erosions. We distinguish the closed core determined by the maximisers of the translation-mass function from the effective support on which the depth exceeds its unavoidable baseline. We establish continuity, affine equivariance, comparison with halfspace (Tukey) depth, and normal-cone and smoothness criteria. For uniform measures on convex bodies, the regions coincide exactly with the ball floating bodies of Schütt, Werner and Yalikun; for positive continuous densities they coincide with the weighted ball floating bodies of Werner and Yalikun. For dilates $tK$, the depth converges to a depth generated by the tangent cones of $K$ as $t \to \infty$; for smooth $K$ this limit is Tukey's halfspace depth, whereas nonsmooth testing bodies can produce a genuinely different limit. The worst-case maximal $K$-depth is exactly $1/h_T(K)$, where $h_T(K)$ is the Helly number of the family of translates of $K$. Under a uniform interior rolling-ball condition and compact support and having zero mass on hyperplanes, the convergence to halfspace depth is monotone and uniform with an explicit error bound. If the density is bounded by $L$, then this bound is of order $O(t^{-1})$ and this order is sharp. We also record that the dependence on the testing body is not monotone in general, while Hausdorff perturbations of $K$ give stable depth functions and regions at regular levels. Finally, we prove uniform consistency and pointwise weak limits for empirical $K$-depth, including the non-Gaussian limit caused by nonunique active translates.

papers.title: How Robust Are Prognostic Radiomic Features? Comparing Selection Techniques on Pooled Glioblastoma Cohorts
papers.abstract: Radiomic survival studies in glioblastoma report heterogeneous prognostic features, but how much of this stems from the methodology itself is rarely examined. We analysed the association of 463 radiomic, anatomical and clinical features from pre-treatment MRI with overall survival in 705 IDH-wildtype glioblastoma patients from three public cohorts, using three techniques: a log-rank test after median split, univariate Cox regression (both Benjamini-Hochberg corrected) and an XGBoost regressor interpreted with SHAP. The log-rank test selected 99 features, Cox regression 72 and SHAP its top 20; five were selected by all three: age, a peritumoural T2 texture feature, the number of connected peritumoural mask components and two image-level intensity maxima. The two survival tests shared 51 features, about half of the SHAP top 20 were also selected by either test, and where selections overlapped, effect directions agreed. Many selections were PyRadiomics diagnostic descriptors that are not restricted to tumour voxels. Analytical pipeline choices, including ranking method, pre-filtering and descriptor handling, can substantially influence which features appear prognostic.

papers.title: Sensitivity Analysis for Multivariate Optimal Sample Allocation
papers.abstract: Optimal sample allocation in stratified surveys for a single characteristic is well understood, yet multivariate allocation remains challenging. In the absence of a total order on the precision vector, a decision-maker must balance competing objectives through preference weightings whose effects on the resulting allocation are generally unclear. This paper develops an analytical sensitivity analysis for multivariate optimal allocation based on the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions. We show that a stepwise weighted Chebyshev minimisation yields a unique efficient allocation and the normal vector to the Pareto frontier, from which marginal rates of substitution between survey objectives and shadow prices for cost and precision constraints follow directly. The method enables interpretable adjustments to weightings or cost limits when specified allocations do not meet survey purposes. Numerical results on an educational survey quantify the impact of budget and quality constraints on estimation precision and demonstrate how the trade-off information guides iterative refinement of preference weightings.

papers.title: Financial Literacy and the Functional Shape of Subjective Time Deformation in Intertemporal Choice
papers.abstract: Intertemporal decisions are commonly summarized by a single discount parameter, although individuals with similar overall discounting intensity may value short-, medium-, and long-term delays differently. This study investigates whether financial literacy is associated with these horizon-specific differences by treating reconstructed subjective time as a functional rather than scalar outcome. Data were collected through a multilingual online questionnaire administered to a convenience and snowball sample of 140 adults, who provided hypothetical equivalence judgments for a future reward of EUR 100 over 13 horizons from 7 days to 5 years, a three-item financial-literacy measure, and measures of temporal perception. Individual discount trajectories were reconstructed and analyzed with function-on-scalar regression, allowing the association with financial literacy to vary across the temporal domain. Because the normalized subjective-time trajectory is not identifiable for flat or reconstruction-degenerate discount profiles, the primary functional analysis included 59 participants, while complementary analyses used the full analytical sample. The primary model provided no evidence of a robust linear association between financial literacy and subjective-time deformation. An exploratory categorical specification indicated heterogeneity across financial-literacy levels and departure from a linear-score representation, although individual contrasts were imprecise and sensitive to specification. The relationship between financial literacy and intertemporal valuation may thus be more complex than a monotonic score effect, and functional data analytics can reveal horizon-specific structure that scalar summaries obscure. Given the convenience sample and the reduced identified sample, the results are exploratory and require validation in larger independent samples.

papers.title: Mediation and moderation in distance-based regression with triangular fuzzy data: simulation evidence and an application to academic performance
papers.abstract: We study mediation and moderation in the distance-based regression model for triangular fuzzy responses, in which the center and transformed spreads of the response are linear in the components of fuzzy and crisp covariates. With a common design, componentwise least squares minimizes the unconstrained quadratic extension of the Yang--Ko distance on the transformed scale, for any choice of its shape parameters. Direct, indirect and total effects are defined separately for the center and the spreads of the response as plug-in contrasts on the fitted equations; when the mediator spreads are transformed and carry part of the indirect association, the product-of-coefficients rule no longer holds for the center. Moderation is modeled through triangular interaction regressors and tested with a Freedman--Lane permutation test. In simulations calibrated on real data, percentile bootstrap intervals for the indirect effects had coverage between 0.905 and 0.975, the empirical size of the indirect-effect tests did not exceed 0.085, and ignoring the paths through the mediator spreads biased the indirect effect on the center by 16 to 20\% at every sample size. The fuzzy model predicted better than a centers-only model only from $n=250$. In data on 91 university students collected in 2014, the indirect contrast through a course indicator accounted for about half of the model-based association between prior knowledge and the center of academic performance, the interactions of prior knowledge with sex and with motivation remained after a Holm adjustment, and the spreads of the covariates did not improve leave-one-out prediction.

papers.title: Federated Community Detection in Bipartite Networks
papers.abstract: We study federated spectral estimation when a large matrix is horizontally partitioned across servers that cannot share raw data. We propose FLICKER, a target-specific gradient-based power iteration that recovers a singular direction associated with a prescribed spectral target using only matrix-vector products on local blocks. Different target directions can be recovered independently and in parallel. We establish non-asymptotic convergence guarantees and provide a recursive grid-search procedure for spectral target selection. Building on FLICKER, we develop BiFLICKER for federated community detection in bipartite networks, together with a sequential projected variant for nearby or repeated singular directions. Under a sparse bipartite stochastic block model, we show that properly rescaled leading singular values from a reference server provide valid global targets, and that Sequential BiFLICKER achieves a vanishing misclustering rate and exact recovery under stronger sparsity conditions. Simulations show that BiFLICKER remains close to centralized spectral clustering and is more robust than existing federated spectral baselines when local sample sizes are small. On a LastFM user-artist network naturally partitioned by country, Sequential BiFLICKER attains an overall ARI of 0.94 against centralized clustering while revealing cross-country communities with distinct listening profiles.

papers.title: Tuning-Free Tests for Treatment Effect Heterogeneity via Expectile Processes
papers.abstract: This paper develops tuning-free tests for treatment-effect heterogeneity. By characterizing the null hypothesis as constancy of the expectile treatment-effect curve, we construct test statistics as continuous functionals of the mean-centered sample expectile process. We establish a uniform Bahadur representation, derive the asymptotic properties of the test statistics under the null and fixed alternatives, and show nontrivial power against local alternatives approaching the null at the $n^{-1/2}$ rate. For feasible inference, we develop a fast multiplier bootstrap that consistently approximates the nonpivotal null distribution while capturing the first-order effect of estimating the unknown common shift. The procedure is tuning-free, requiring no density or score-function estimation, bandwidth selection, or repeated refitting. The framework further incorporates a pointwise-studentized refinement and a covariate adjustment that reduces asymptotic variation without altering the population discrepancy. Monte Carlo comparisons with existing methods show generally reliable size control, competitive power, and substantial computational savings. An application to a large-scale water-conservation experiment illustrates the proposed tests.

papers.title: Keep the Lineages Alive: Diversity-Preserving SMC for Diffusion LLM Decoding
papers.abstract: Inference-time sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding can improve the reasoning accuracy of masked diffusion language models (diffusion LLMs) without post-training by resampling a population of partial generations according to a reward. Its effectiveness therefore depends on the resampling step, which must concentrate computation on promising candidates while retaining enough diversity to explore alternative reasoning paths. The reward can be internal, the decoder's own confidence on the committed prefix, or external, a process reward model scoring that prefix. Under either reward, multinomial resampling can disrupt this balance by duplicating high-weight particles and discarding lineages that may still reach a correct solution. The effective sample size (ESS) does not register this loss: multinomial resampling resets it to its maximum even as distinct lineages disappear. To retain such lineages, we introduce lineage-preserving SMC (LP-SMC), which combines Chopthin resampling with an input weight floor. Instead of equalizing weights, Chopthin bounds the ratio between the largest and smallest weights it returns and carries the unequal weights forward. The floor limits how far below the maximum a weight may fall before resampling so that lineages with low early weight keep a chance to recover. Across mathematical-reasoning and code-generation benchmarks on two base models, LP-SMC raises oracle coverage, the fraction of problems with at least one correct particle, in every setting, by 1.8 to 25.6 points, and raises end-to-end accuracy under a common reward-model selector in eleven of twelve settings, by up to 7.9 points on LLaDA-1.5 and 18.3 on Dream-7B. The coverage gain persists under the external reward model, which suggests that diversity-preserving resampling and the guidance signal contribute separately to inference-time search.

papers.title: Where to weight? Estimating population causal effects with weighted double score matching in complex surveys
papers.abstract: Double score matching is an emerging method for causal inference that combines propensity and prognostic scores to achieve dimension reduction and model robustness. However, when the observational data are drawn from a complex survey, the existing literature does not provide sufficient guidance on the proper use of survey weights in matching strategies for population-level causal inference. We develop weighted double score matching (WDSM) that provides a unified framework for incorporating survey weights throughout the score estimation, matching, and outcome analysis under both retrospective (informative) and prospective (non-informative) sampling designs. We establish asymptotic normality of the resultant effect estimates under both known and estimated scores and develop a linearization-based bootstrap procedure for variance estimation that preserves the survey-weighted matching structure. Simulation studies show that WDSM substantially reduces bias relative to unweighted matching when either the propensity score model or the prognostic score models are correctly specified. Under correct specification, WDSM also improves efficiency and confidence interval coverage relative to survey-weighted propensity score matching, with particularly pronounced gains under poor overlap. Applications to early marijuana use and mental health in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health and to sleep duration and glycemic control in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey illustrate the practical value of WDSM for population-level inference. We conclude with a discussion of our findings and provide practical guidance on incorporating survey weights into matching-based analyses of observational data.

papers.title: Optimal Priors for Betting Tests with Bounded Payoffs: An Exact Efficiency Characterization
papers.abstract: Testing by betting is a powerful framework that recasts hypothesis testing as a betting game. A popular approach uses an $F$-weighted portfolio with a predefined prior $F$. For suitable priors, this approach has recently been shown to achieve the optimal expected rejection time as the error probability goes to zero at a fixed alternative. Yet, the prior $F$ changes how the portfolio test behaves near the null. This motivates the question: Which prior should we use in testing-by-betting algorithms? We study bounded scalar payoffs and introduce an efficiency measure that allows the error probability and alternative to vary jointly. Under mild assumptions, we prove that efficiency equals a logarithmic decay index of the prior near zero. This gives a necessary and sufficient condition for optimality: Beta priors have infinite efficiency, whereas suitable Robbins-type priors attain efficiency 1. As an application, we consider testing a specified mean of a bounded random variable and describe an implementation of the portfolio algorithm with almost-linear computational complexity.

papers.title: A multivariate index for estimating seasonal shifts from temperature curves
papers.abstract: Seasonal timing is often studied using fixed calendar seasons, temperature thresholds, or a fixed smoothing parameter applied across all years. These may be sensitive to changes in variability over time. To address this, we propose the Seasonal Adaptive LocalisabLe Index (SALLI), a multivariate index, for characterising seasonality from daily temperature curves observed over complete seasons. SALLI uses Significant Zero Crossings of Derivatives (SiZer) to identify significant increases and decreases across a range of smoothing levels. It uses this information to select a smoothing level for each year. The method assumes one main warm peak and one cool trough per annual cycle. For each year, SALLI estimates the annual temperature curve and the midpoints of the four seasons and temperatures. These estimates describe changes in both seasonal timing and temperature. We illustrate SALLI using Australian maximum temperature data from 1965 to 2024. Comparisons of SALLI estimates over the first and last decades show not only a warming, but a shift to earlier seasons, with the midpoints of spring, summer, and winter occurring roughly a week earlier. All four seasonal midpoints become warmer, with the largest increases occurring in summer (1.37 $^\circ$C) and spring (1.22 $^\circ$C). Warming is evident across time, whereas the clearest shift in seasonal timing emerges after the 2000s. By estimating both timing and temperature at each seasonal midpoint, SALLI locates where changes occur on the annual temperature curve, providing information that is more robust and data-driven than fixed thresholds, fixed calendar seasons, or a single smoothing choice.

papers.title: Using Bayesian Sequential Logistic Regression to Model the Organ Transplant Selection Process
papers.abstract: Organ transplantation evaluation is a multi-stage process in which only patients who complete one stage remain eligible for the next, leading to patient attrition and reducing later-stage sample sizes. Covariate associations may differ across decision points, and identifying these stage-specific effects is necessary to target interventions and understand disparities. Conventional approaches that model each transition independently fail to distinguish stage-specific from shared associations and tend to produce imprecise estimates at later stages. We propose a Bayesian sequential logistic regression (BSLR) framework that represents progression as conditional Bernoulli distributions within a joint likelihood that preserves chronological ordering; we further show its equivalence to an adjusted continuation-ratio model. A hierarchical prior decomposes each covariate effect into an overall effect and a transition-specific deviation. This partial-pooling structure shares information across stages and stabilizes estimation where data are sparse, while a masking mechanism accommodates covariates structurally unavailable at particular stages without discarding records or imputing values. In simulations, BSLR achieved lower bias, posterior variance, and mean squared error than independent logistic regression. We demonstrated the utility of our model using a cohort of patients referred for kidney or liver transplant. Posterior estimates indicated that the associations of clinical indicators and social determinants of health with progression differed across care continuum phases. BSLR identified stage-specific heterogeneity in covariate associations, revealing factors whose effects reversed direction across evaluation stages and detecting associations at late-stage transitions that independent models failed to resolve due to insufficient precision.

papers.title: Estimation and Inference for the Joint Autoregressive Quantile-Expected Shortfall Model
papers.abstract: Expected shortfall is defined as the truncated mean of a random variable that falls below a specified quantile level and is widely recognized as an important risk measure. Motivated by the empirical observation of clustering patterns in financial risks, we consider a joint autoregressive model for both conditional quantile and expected shortfall. Existing estimation methods for such models typically rely on minimizing a nonlinear and nonconvex joint loss function, which is challenging to solve. We introduce a two-step regression framework to estimate the model parameters with theoretical guarantees. We further develop a Portmanteau test for model diagnostics and prove its asymptotic validity for Type I error control. Our empirical results on stock market data indicate that the proposed models effectively capture the clustering patterns and leverage effects on the conditional expected shortfall.

papers.title: A LATE-Targeting Experimental Design for Multi-Arm RCTs
papers.abstract: We study the design of multi-arm experiments that identify local average treatment effects under imperfect compliance. With three or more arms, conventional randomization fails to identify margin-specific effects even under strong extensions of monotone compliance. A choice-theoretic analysis unifies these extensions and motivates a two-stage design: subjects report a preferred arm and are randomized conditional on it. If treatment is confined to the assigned or reported arm, one-sided noncompliance is restored conditional on the report, identifying the effect between the two for their compliers. We discuss the design's applicability and feasibility in relation to the choice model.

papers.title: A Bayesian Distance-Weighted Ising Model for Task-Related Regional Analysis of Neuroimaging Data
papers.abstract: Neuroimaging analysis commonly involves classifying cognitive conditions, identifying task-relevant brain regions, and examining functional connectivity. These objectives are typically addressed separately, without a model-based framework. In contrast, we propose a Bayesian distance-weighted Ising model that integrates classification, regional importance, and connectivity analysis. The model captures dependence among task labels based on connectivities between functional signals, while region-of-interest (ROI)-specific interaction parameters account for spatial heterogeneity and quantify regional contributions to task discrimination. However, inference is challenging because the signals may be observed on unequal time grids and the likelihood function contains an intractable normalising constant. To address this, we use a basis expansion and an auxiliary variable Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm. We apply the method to functional near-infrared spectroscopy data from younger and older adults, comparing resting-state and task-related activity. The model achieves high classification accuracy and reveals age-dependent patterns of regional importance and connectivity. Among younger adults, the left orbitofrontal cortex contributes more strongly to task discrimination than the dorsolateral prefrontal and frontopolar cortices, whereas regional differences are less evident among older adults. Older adults also exhibit greater bilateral connectivity between corresponding ROIs, consistent with reduced hemispheric lateralisation.

papers.title: Anytime-Valid Inference in Linear Models with Clustered Outcomes: Exact Multivariate Tests and Cluster-Robust Confidence Sequences
papers.abstract: We extend anytime-valid inference for linear models from independent scalar outcomes to units that contribute a vector of dependent outcomes. We develop a parametric and a nonparametric treatment. For the Gaussian multivariate linear model with an unstructured error covariance, we derive a closed-form Bayes factor under the right-Haar prior and a matrix-normal mixture alternative and prove that it is an exact e-value at every sample size and a test martingale in the invariant filtration. To our knowledge, this Bayes factor is new in the generality considered here: a d x q coefficient matrix, nuisance regressors and an arbitrary fixed positive-definite prior precision under the right-Haar nuisance prior. It yields sequential Hotelling and MANOVA tests with exact confidence sequences. Under a common within-cluster design, the cluster-robust Wald statistic of a pooled regression is equal to Hotelling's T^2 statistic computed from the per-cluster least-squares summaries, giving an exact Gaussian benchmark with G-1 degrees of freedom. For general clustered population least-squares projections, the corresponding sandwich statistic is an asymptotic e-process, without Gaussian, common-design or linearity assumptions. Each treatment includes growth and first-order expected stopping-time results; under stronger regularity, direct comparisons of expected log evidence identify a fixed mixture precision that maximizes expected log growth through constant order within a specified family, for a specified frequentist alternative. Applied to randomized experiments with several outcomes, the robust procedure gives asymptotically anytime-valid joint tests, confidence ellipsoids and simultaneous confidence sequences for the vector of average treatment effects from ordinary least-squares estimates and cluster-robust standard errors.

papers.title: Linear Regression with Common Unobserved Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: We study inference on common slope parameters in linear panel models with two-way unobserved heterogeneity. In linear regression, bias arises from unobserved heterogeneity that is shared between the residual and the covariates. Our common unobserved heterogeneity (CUH) estimator targets this common variation directly: it searches over functionals of the residualised outcome for variation that also resides in the covariates, and seeks to further project out only bias-inducing variation. This makes the estimator less sensitive to weak outcome factors while avoiding the complete removal of exogenous variation in covariates that is unrelated to the confounding heterogeneity. We develop a weak-factor theory based on a singular-value strength index and establish $\sqrt{NT}$-asymptotic normality of the cross-fitted CUH estimator. Under homoskedastic errors, its asymptotic variance is no larger than that of a common correlated effects factor estimator. Simulations and empirical applications illustrate the resulting bias--variance trade-off and the gains from selectively removing common variation.

papers.title: Probabilistic Limit Order Book Forecasting with Conditional Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Modeling limit order book (LOB) dynamics is central to market forecasting and execution-strategy evaluation. While diffusion models achieve strong empirical performance, existing LOB snapshot models typically lack a learned recurrent encoder and formal statistical guarantees. We introduce LOBGrad, a conditional DDPM framework for probabilistic LOB forecasting that combines an autoregressive RNN encoder with a diffusion-based generator. In particular, we establish an excess-risk oracle inequality for the one-step DDPM noise-prediction objective under exponential mixing and regularity assumptions. We further show that, under contractive dynamics, the dependence on the conditioning-window length can be reduced to a dependence on the latent-state dimension. Experiments on BTC/USDT, GOOGL, and META show that LOBGrad improves on its encoder-free diffusion ablation across all reported queue metrics and obtains competitive results against other baselines. It also reproduces the key stylized facts of LOB microstructure, and yields reasonably calibrated queue-based predictive intervals. A stylized downstream task illustrates the potential value of the generated forecasts.

papers.title: Multivariate M-extremiles
papers.abstract: Extremiles represent an important class of distributional functionals defined through weighted squared loss functions, providing a valuable alternative to quantiles and expectiles. To date, their development has remained confined to the univariate setting. Here we introduce a robust multivariate extension of extremiles for random vectors by combining a directional weighting mechanism with Huber's multidimensional loss function. The proposed definition yields a family of directional extremiles indexed by a tuning parameter controlling the degree of robustness to outliers, with the quadratic-loss geometric extremile arising as a limiting case. We prove their main theoretical properties and introduce the notion of extremile sets. From an inferential perspective, we develop an efficient two-step procedure based on iteratively reweighted least squares, and derive asymptotic properties using the theory of Z-estimators. The finite-sample behavior of the proposed methodology is investigated through simulation experiments under Gaussian, contaminated, and heavy-tailed settings. An application to daily returns of three major cryptocurrencies illustrates its practical utility on financial data.

papers.title: Sensitivity Analysis for Trials with Irregular and Informative Assessment Times: Marginal Mean Models and Sensitivity Parameter Selection
papers.abstract: In randomized trials, outcome assessment times often vary across participants and may depend on the underlying outcome process, so outcomes observed near a target time need not represent the target population. Whether assessment is informative cannot be determined from the observed data alone. We extend the sensitivity analysis framework of Smith et al.\ (2024), which is anchored in an explainable assessment assumption and was restricted to continuous outcomes through an identity-link marginal mean model, to a broader class of link functions that accommodates binary and count outcomes. Within this framework, we develop an influence function-based augmented inverse intensity-weighted estimator that is root-$n$ consistent under standard regularity conditions. We also propose a data-driven procedure for selecting the range of the sensitivity parameter from plausible bounds on the target mean outcome and for constructing a confidence set for this range, which accounts for uncertainty in sensitivity parameter selection. We illustrate the method with data from the ARC study and evaluate its finite-sample performance in simulation studies.

papers.title: Inference on Linear Programs via Feasibility Testing
papers.abstract: This paper studies inference on the value of a linear program (LP) when the objective and constraints are estimated. Using LP duality, we construct one- and two-sided confidence intervals by inverting tests of the feasibility of systems of linear inequalities. Existing tests yield asymptotically valid confidence intervals but can have poor power. We propose a modification that augments these systems with estimated ``box constraints.'' The resulting procedure has power against $N^{-1/2}$-local alternatives and yields confidence intervals of order $N^{-1/2}$. These results require only that the LP value be finite, and do not require compactness of the feasible region nor standard constraint qualifications. We obtain stronger guarantees under various constraint qualifications and establish uniform validity over large classes of DGPs when known deterministic constraints bound the primal and/or dual variables. Simulations demonstrate good finite-sample performance.

papers.title: Bias correcting transaction cost models for characteristic function based estimators
papers.abstract: Effective transaction cost is a necessary step for devising any competing financial trading strategy in the absence of quote data. Classically, Roll's model estimated the transaction cost using the first order autocovariance of the difference between daily transaction prices, while Hasbrouck's Bayesian approach used iterative posterior simulation. However, Roll's model fails when the first order autocovariance becomes positive, while Hasbrouck's estimator is computationally intensive, especially when many securities are involved. We develop empirical characteristic function methods with a first order bias correcting for spread estimation, and establish the asymptotic distribution of the corrected estimator under suitable conditions. Our numerical experiments illustrate the bias-variance tradeoff of characteristic-function methods compared to Roll's model, and their computational advantage over Hasbrouck's model.

papers.title: Efficient estimation of measures of functional dependence
papers.abstract: Measures of functional dependence that characterize both independence and perfect dependence have attracted growing interest. Despite their appealing theoretical properties, existing rank- and graph-based estimators can suffer from substantial bias under general dependence, limiting their usefulness for statistical inference. Moreover, a systematic and practically accessible framework for mitigating such bias while achieving semiparametric efficiency remains largely unavailable. In this paper, we develop a general framework for efficient estimation of measures of functional dependence through sample-splitting and cross-fitting. Our approach enables systematic bias reduction and semiparametrically efficient inference, and thus offers a flexible and theoretically grounded alternative to existing rank- and graph-based methods.

papers.title: DR-Learners for Generalizing CATEs from a Randomized Controlled Trial
papers.abstract: Randomized clinical trials are essential for evaluating interventions, yet average treatment effects can obscure treatment effect heterogeneity, making conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) a natural target. However, restrictive eligibility criteria and differential trial participation can limit the generalizability of these effects to broader target populations. Building on existing DR-Learners, we develop the gDR-Learner for generalizing RCT CATEs to a target population, using cross-fitted machine-learning nuisance estimation. We derive excess-risk bounds in which nuisance errors enter only as products, showing that the estimator achieves oracle-rate convergence despite slower individual nuisance estimation. The variables needed to generalize are rarely measured across the entire target population. We therefore extend the methods to two settings with incomplete covariate information: when certain covariates are measured only in the trial (e.g., biomarkers), and covariates driving trial participation measured only in a subsample of the target population, such as a representative cohort or registry. We construct weighted conformal prediction intervals for individual treatment effects, accounting for covariate shift between the trial and target population. In simulations, the gDR-Learner achieved the lowest estimation error when all covariates were observed relative to standard T- and DR-Learners and an inverse-probability-weighted T-Learner, and also outperformed the latter under incomplete covariate observation. We illustrate the methods by reanalyzing the Coronary Artery Surgery Study, examining treatment effect heterogeneity by prior myocardial infarction and baseline ejection fraction.

papers.title: The Hidden Look-Ahead: Point-in-Time Leakage in Electricity Market Data
papers.abstract: Empirical studies of electricity prices routinely state that their models use only information available at the time of the trading decision. For weather-driven forecasts drawn from commercial archives, this condition is harder to meet than it appears, and whether it holds can change over time. We identify three timing pitfalls. A forecast run is labelled by the issue time of its weather model, but becomes available hours later and keeps changing after publication. Auction gates follow local clock time, while archives use UTC. Outturn series are revised after publication without earlier values being kept. Using the timestamps of 128,656 forecast runs from ten weather-model configurations, matched to the day-ahead and first intraday auction gates in Great Britain over 2022-2026, we find that selecting "the latest run issued before the gate" picks a run not yet published at the gate on more than 99% of delivery days for six of the ten configurations at one of the two gates. For GFS at the day-ahead gate, the share is 0.6% in winter and 99.8% in summer. The exposure also shifts as publication delays drift, and an action margin of a few minutes can cost a full six-hour forecast cycle. The wrongly selected inputs differ materially from those available at the gate, but their apparent accuracy gain ranges from -9% to +24% across variables, models, gates and seasons, so its effect cannot be assumed and must be measured. We argue that point-in-time correctness is a dynamic property of the data pipeline, and propose a protocol that audits it from timestamps before any model is fitted.

papers.title: State Space Modeling of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Process with Measurement Error: An Application to Microbiome Data
papers.abstract: Understanding the temporal dynamics of the human microbiome is critical for deciphering host-microbe interactions and identifying responses to environmental or physiological disruptions. In this study, we develop a likelihood-based framework grounded in Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) state-space modeling to analyze longitudinal microbiome data. By applying log-ratio transformations to genus-level relative abundances, we accommodate the compositional nature of microbiome profiles and enable biologically interpretable inference. We estimate the mean reversion rate of the OU process using maximum likelihood estimation and construct profile likelihood confidence intervals to assess temporal stability. Biologically, higher estimated mean-reversion rates correspond to stronger regulatory feedback and thus greater temporal stability of the gut microbiome, whereas lower rates reflect weaker stabilization and slower recovery from perturbations. In the datasets analyzed here, most estimated mean reversion rates were between 0.12 and 0.36, corresponding to a half-life in the range 2-6 days for the system to return to the equilibrium level. These mean-reversion rates are substantially lower than previous estimates obtained from OU models that did not account for measurement error. To capture structural shifts in microbial dynamics, we propose a statistical testing procedure that compares a single-parameter model to a split-parameter model across disrupted time periods. We also propose an OUSSM to jointly model multiple microbes, taking into account the special measurement error covariance structure for log-ratio transformed data.

papers.title: Estimating Causal Bounds from Observational Data With Neural Generative Models
papers.abstract: Identifying causal bounds from discrete observational data is a fundamental problem in causal inference. While exact analytical bounds exist for certain graphs, this is not generally the case. In this paper, we introduce a framework for estimating such bounds using neural generative models together with a new extrapolation procedure to estimate these bounds more accurately. Across multiple causal inference settings, it produces bounds that are consistently closer to the true bounds than those obtained with existing general neural approaches. We validate the framework on a range of benchmark problems for which exact bounds are available.

papers.title: Persistence is not Independence: A structural Credibility Protocol for Distribution based Recovery in VARLiNGAM
papers.abstract: VAR-LiNGAM recovers a contemporaneous structure from reduced-form innovations under mutual independence of the underlying structural shocks. Recovery itself and bootstrap stability of the recovered edges are natural post-estimation outputs, but neither directly assesses the identifying independence assumption. We organize post-recovery validation as an ordered, non-compensatory protocol with four layers (reduced-form admissibility, distributional informativeness, independence support and edge persistence) and establish, by a constructive population result, a Monte Carlo experiment under known ground truth and a firm-level Compustat application, that the last two layers are non-nested: an edge can persist under resampling while the recovered shocks remain dependent, and independence can be supported while the leading recovered edge fails to persist. Independence support is classified operationally by a block-permutation dHSIC diagnostic on the recovered shocks, with mutual information as a continuous measure of residual dependence and tail co-exceedance as a complementary extreme-dependence diagnostic. Empirically, the conjunction of no detected independence violation and a reportable persistent leading edge occurs only in a small subset.

papers.title: Conventional Inference under Nonstationary Heavy Tailed Fractional Processes & Arrays
papers.abstract: Existing regression inference methods for nonstationary heavy tailed data are largely limited to unit roots tests. Functional central limit theorems (FCLTs), which are commonly used for the asymptotic analysis of nonstationary models, are inapplicable to nonstationary data characterized by a memory parameter $d<1$ and a stability parameter $α<2$. Furthermore, it is well known that inference under nonstationarity is often non-conventional, and this issue is exacerbated in the presence of heavy-tailed data. The interaction of long memory and heavy tails significantly enlarges the nonstationary region---i.e., the covariate model space---where conventional inference methods typically fail. To address these challenges, we propose a new limit theory and methods that facilitate both workable asymptotics and conventional inference in regressions involving general nonstationary heavy-tailed covariate processes. Specifically, our approach develops a limit theory for heavy-tailed weakly nonstationary processes (hereafter, HT-WNPs), which lie on the threshold of nonstationarity (cf. Duffy and Kasparis, 2021, Annals of Statistics). We demonstrate that the proposed methods---including IVX-based and related instrumental-variable procedures---facilitate conventional inference for a broad class of stationary and nonstationary heavy-tailed covariates. This class includes nearly and mildly integrated arrays, as well as nonstationary fractional processes with memory parameter $1-1/α<d<2-1/α$, where $α\in(1,2]$. Our analysis is applicable to both parametric and kernel regression models. The finite-sample performance of the proposed methods is evaluated through a comprehensive simulation study. Additionally, we provide an empirical application to the predictability of stock returns using long-memory heavy-tailed predictors.

papers.title: Vector Copula-Based Markov Models
papers.abstract: We propose the Vector Copula-based Markov Model (VCBMM) for describing multivariate time series with nonlinear dependence. To extend univariate copula-based Markov models to multivariate time series, we develop a hierarchical construction based on scalar aggregates and consider the Vector Sklar Theorem to obtain the joint density of the VCBMM. We further assume the Clayton copula for serial dependence and the multivariate Gaussian distribution for the marginals. The corresponding likelihood function and Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) with the Inference Functions for Margins (IFM) method are provided. The performance of the proposed model is illustrated through simulation studies. In real data analysis, we apply the model to bivariate daily stock returns from the 2008 global financial crisis (2008 GFC) and the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic (2020 COVID-19).

papers.title: Spontaneous brain-wide rotational dynamics constrain cue-evoked behavior
papers.abstract: Uncovering low-dimensional representations of brain-wide neural dynamics and their relationship to behavior remains a central challenge. Here, we show that spontaneous brain-wide rotational dynamics constrain cue-evoked behavior and learning. To systematically establish these findings, we developed a dimensionality-reduction technique called Rotational Component Analysis (RCA) that optimizes the detection of low-variance rotational modes even within individual trials. We applied RCA to motor-cortical spike-train data from monkeys and humans, mouse cortex-wide calcium imaging, and human functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and magnetoencephalography (MEG). In mice, a rotational mode identified from activity recorded at rest predicts cue-evoked behavior: the phase of rotation when a randomly timed cue arrives predicts whether the animal subsequently pulls the lever. We explain this surprisingly strong correlation using both a recurrent neural network (RNN) and a minimal two-dimensional model of response learning, in which the intrinsic rotational mode serves as a dynamical constraint on response and learning. We further identify double-rotation modes containing two centers of rotation that separate preparatory from task dynamics in both mouse and human data. Remarkably, corresponding modes also organize neural dynamics during a non-motor human task, and rotational irreversibility captures early psychosis even when principal component analysis shows no group difference. Our work establishes rotational dynamics as low-dimensional coordinates that constrain how ongoing brain states are converted into behavior. More broadly, RCA provides a versatile tool for detecting hidden nonreciprocal dynamics in biological and physical datasets.

papers.title: Globally Optimal Estimation of Nested Logit Models
papers.abstract: Nested logit is widely used in operational demand models, yet jointly estimating its utility coefficients and nest dissimilarity parameters requires nonconvex optimization. Standard estimation routines offer no certificate of global optimality, leaving a gap between globally optimizing decisions under nested-logit demand and reliably estimating that demand model. We develop, to our knowledge, the first globally convergent optimization framework with an explicit global-accuracy guarantee for joint nested-logit estimation. Our central complexity result confines all exponential dependence to the number of free nest dissimilarity parameters: computation is polynomial in the numbers of observations, alternatives, and utility coefficients. Consequently, under the stated compact-domain and relaxation-error conditions, fixing the number of nests yields an additive polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS). The framework exploits an exact exponential-cone formulation for fixed dissimilarities and a spatial branch-and-bound algorithm that searches only over the free dissimilarities. Valid likelihood bounds provide an anytime certificate and finite termination at any prescribed additive average-log-likelihood tolerance. Across eight benchmark datasets and 240 estimation instances, the method certifies every reported solution and exposes inferior local estimates despite normal solver termination. These results establish a computational foundation for globally certified nested-logit estimation.

papers.title: Nonparametric Dyadic Quantile Regression
papers.abstract: This paper considers nonparametric quantile regression for directed dyadic data observed on the ordered pairs of a complete network with n vertices. The observations exhibit dyadic dependence: dyads with disjoint indices are independent, whereas dyads sharing one or two indices are correlated. The local linear smoothing technique is adopted to estimate the quantile regression function. The asymptotic theory reveals that convergence rates of the proposed dyadic quantile regression estimation crucially depend on whether degeneracy occurs for the underlying network generating process. A rate-adaptive standardized version of the limit distribution is derived under some mild conditions. In addition, an easy-to-implement method is proposed to estimate the asymptotic variance of nonparametric dyadic quantile regression estimation. The finite-sample performance and applicability of the proposed methodology are illustrated with Monte-Carlo simulation and a real data application to bilateral portfolio holdings.
